Chapter 5: Memory, Imagination, and the Ongoing Search for Justice.
When it comes to searching for Ali, it’s not just about piecing together a few scattered facts, or simply correcting the historical record. This journey is ongoing—it asks us to draw on both memory and imagination.
Think about what it really means to reconstruct a life that’s been forgotten. It’s an act of empathy. You’re trying to step into someone else’s shoes, to see the world through their eyes, to imagine what they hoped for, what they feared, the moments that brought them joy, or the ones that weighed them down.
Let’s be honest, this work isn’t easy. The records are scattered, sometimes barely there at all. Some days, it feels like the trail just disappears, making you wonder if it’s even possible to know what really happened. But then, there are those special moments—a small detail or a half-remembered story that suddenly brings the past vividly to life. In those moments, remembering becomes an act of honoring. It’s about giving a voice, and a place, to those who’ve been left out of the narrative.
Imagination is absolutely crucial here. It lets us look beyond what’s written in the official accounts, to fill in the blanks with empathy and understanding. And no, it’s not about making things up. It’s about recognizing that we’ll never know everything, and being willing to accept the complexity that comes with that. Searching for Ali reminds us that history is never complete—it always needs to be revisited, revised, and renewed.
And then, there’s the question of justice. It’s always right there, just beneath the surface. To remember Ali means facing the legacy of colonialism head-on. It means asking, what does it really take to do justice to people whose lives have been pushed to the margins? It’s not just about acknowledging them or putting their names in a footnote. It’s about changing the way we tell history, and even the way science is done. It’s about building a more honest and inclusive story—one that truly values everyone’s contributions.
The story of Ali and Wallace isn’t just about things that happened long ago. It speaks to where we are right now, and to the struggles that are still happening for recognition and justice. It’s a powerful reminder that the work of remembering never really ends. Every step we take to recover what’s been lost is also a step toward hope.
In the end, the search for Ali is a search for a better way of seeing the world—a way that honors the many lives and stories that shape our understanding, and refuses to let anyone fade into obscurity.
